It's rather sweet but also feels aimless and thin.

As director, Zora invests the fraught verbal engagements between the two women with tension, but the constant resort to soliloquy – one or other character unpacking the last argument or preparing us for the next one – becomes tiresome and saps this 90-minute play of energy.
An overly neat ending and a general nagging sense that this is a play written for Broadway – that is to say, a bit too sleek, a bit too streamlined – perhaps hold the writing back from greatness.
It becomes something else – a surprising and quietly powerful study of grief and families.
But its emotional honesty hits home, beautifully served by Hille and Kellyman.
But it’s an unremarkable story and the turn-taking monologues start to feel tediously self-indulgent towards the end of the play's 90-minute run-time.
But if this is a wisp of a drama, these two actors give its gauzy translucency substance.
Afternoon covers familiar familial tensions, maybe not with buckets of originality, but with plenty of evocative charm.
In its restraint lies its impact: a finely made play, delivered with a level of care and craft that makes its modest scale feel genuinely rewarding.
Ultimately, Afternoon is a reflective, compassionate exploration of a modern family life and a difficult relationship, imperfect in places but aware that understanding must be spoken into being.
Ultimately, the script is too comfortable to have any impact.
Afternoon tries to do too many things at the same time, drawing in lightly explored mental health challenges.
